About me

I started as a software engineer at Infosys, building enterprise applications for US clients. Somewhere along the way I got curious about why we were building what we were building — so I started sitting in on client product conversations, trying to understand the business logic behind the code. That curiosity eventually led me to launch Studio Classes, a tutoring marketplace I built from scratch — market research, UX, growth, monetisation, the full loop. That was the moment I knew product management was where I wanted to be.

Twelve years in, my instinct is still the same: understand the full picture before touching the solution. I gravitate toward the intersection of data, systems, and user behaviour — the kind of problems where the right diagnosis is more valuable than the obvious fix. Most of my career has been in marketplaces — agri-commodities, healthcare, adventure travel — where supply and demand dynamics, trust mechanics, and conversion architecture interact in non-obvious ways.

I work best in small, high-ownership environments where PMs are expected to write specs, push back on engineering approaches, define instrumentation upfront, and move fast without losing rigour. The case studies here reflect that way of working. B.Tech from NIT Bhopal, MBA from UCD Smurfit in Dublin.

Case Study 01

Search Overhaul: UX, Filters, Intent & Performance

Guidesly · Series A Adventure Booking Platform · 2025–2026

Phase 1 shipped · Phase 2 approved
0.03%
Session-to-completed-booking conversion before
1.5%
Session-to-completed-booking conversion after Phase 1
50×
Conversion improvement
8s→73s
Avg session duration on search results page
17%→65%
Users scrolling below first fold

The Problem

Phase 1 — The search results page was converting at 0.03% session-to-completed-booking. Filters were static and showed irrelevant options regardless of search context. Pricing was buried. Sort options were missing. Key booking information — availability, trip duration, guest capacity — wasn't visible on guide cards. Users couldn't evaluate options without clicking into each listing.

Fixing these shipped a 50× conversion improvement, taking session-to-completed-booking conversion from 0.03% to 1.5%: relevant contextual filters, sort by price, and all critical booking details visible at the card level.

Phase 2 — With the baseline fixed, the next layer was search intent. UTM data showed a significant volume of queries like "best charter boats" bouncing because the location field had no concept of outdoor activity. This phase — approved and in development — adds an intent layer on top of the improved search experience.

Data Signal

"best charter boats" — high-volume query type with near-zero conversion. The location field had no concept of quality or activity intent, so users bounced immediately.

Root Cause

No second autocomplete layer for outdoor activity intent. The field understood places only — not species, game animals, trip styles, or activity types.

Phase 1 — Shipped

Contextual filters surfaced based on search query, sort by price added, availability and pricing made visible on guide cards — removing the need to click into each listing to evaluate.

Integration Spec — Query Logging Schema (14 fields)

raw_query: Exact string before selection. Captures typos, slang, training data for Phase 3 AI.

query_type: place_selected | intent_selected | direct_search | abandoned

activity_type: fishing | hunting | scuba | snow | water | adventure | tours

result_count: Zero-result identification — weekly report feeds directly to supply team for guide recruitment.

outcome: guide_card_clicked | booking_initiated | bounced | refined_search

privacy: No PII. Sanitisation strips email, phone, and name+location patterns from raw_query before storage.

Live product — Phase 1 in production

Live at guidesly.com

Search results page post Phase 1 — filters evolved from static irrelevant options to contextually relevant filters, sort by price added, key booking information (availability, pricing, trip details) surfaced directly on guide cards. Session-to-completed-booking converting at 1.5% vs 0.03% before.

Phase 2 — Intent layer rollout plan

Week 1
Alignment & engineering briefing. Mapping table drafted across 6 activity categories.
Week 2
Intent layer + browse state built. Query logging live from day one.
Week 3
Edge cases QA'd. Geo-intent validated across all 3 states (granted / denied / failed).
Week 4
First zero-result report to supply team. Unrecognised high-frequency terms flagged.

Measurement approach

Before a line of code was written, I defined scroll depth as a leading indicator alongside session-to-completed-booking conversion rate. The reasoning: bookings data takes weeks to mature at Series A volume, but scroll depth would tell us within days whether the UX changes were landing. I set a specific threshold — 40%+ of users scrolling below the first fold — as the "green signal" before reading conversion data seriously.

Pre-launch: 17% of users scrolled below the first fold. Post-launch: 65% — a 3.8× improvement. The leading indicator moved as predicted. Conversion (session-to-completed-booking) followed: 0.03% → 1.5%. Having the measurement framework agreed upfront also meant no post-launch debate about what counted as success — which matters more than the metric itself at a small team.

Session duration on the SRP moved from 8 seconds to 73 seconds — the clearest signal that users were actually evaluating options rather than bouncing immediately.

Case Study 02

Multi-Trip Cart & Booking Protection: From Single Checkout to Trip Planner

Guidesly · Cart & Insurance · 2025–2026

Shipped · Live at guidesly.com
0→1
Cart built from scratch
2.4×
Average trips per order (up from 1.0 — single checkout baseline)
22%
Insurance attach rate post multi-select redesign
3
Post-booking insurance touchpoints

The problem

Guidesly had no cart — every trip was a single, isolated checkout. A customer planning a 2–3 day trip to Islamorada wanting to book fishing one day and scuba diving the next had to complete two separate checkouts. There was no way to plan or pay for a multi-activity trip in one flow.

On the trust side, guides have a strict cancellation window — if a customer doesn't cancel within it, they lose their booking amount entirely. With no protection layer, booking confidence was low, particularly for high-value trips booked weeks in advance. Customer interviews flagged this as a reason for hesitation, not just post-cancellation friction.

Building a cart from scratch at a Series A required buy-in across engineering, design, and leadership — this was the single largest scope item in the product roadmap at the time. I made the case that a multi-trip cart was not just a UX improvement but a revenue-per-customer lever: customers who planned multi-activity trips had higher booking value and lower refund rates. That framing secured the prioritisation.

Before

Single-trip checkout only. No cart, no multi-activity planning, no insurance. Customers lost their full booking amount if they missed the cancellation window.

After

Multi-trip cart with per-trip pricing breakdown, part-payment option, and booking protection — all in one checkout flow. Customers can plan an entire trip itinerary and pay once.

A/B test insight

Initial yes/no insurance toggle showed a low attach rate. Heap data showed users with near-term bookings or trips still within the refund window skipped it entirely. Redesigned to per-trip selection — users choose which trips to insure individually. Insurance attach rate improved significantly post-change, concentrated on trips booked 14+ days out, exactly where cancellation risk is highest.

Post-booking recovery

For users who skipped insurance at checkout — insurance offer sent via booking confirmation page, confirmation email, and SMS on the day the guide's refund window expires.

Key design decisions

Per-trip insurance selection, not a blanket toggle. A customer with one trip booked 2 days out (likely within refund window) and one booked 6 weeks out (likely not) shouldn't have to insure both or neither. The redesigned insurance section shows each trip individually with its insurance cost and lets the user choose which to protect. An explicit "I don't need insurance" option removes ambiguity and reduces friction for confident decliners.

Part-payment model. The cart shows a "Due now" vs "Due later" split — customers pay a deposit at checkout and the balance closer to the trip date. This reduces upfront commitment and improves conversion on high-value bookings. Engineering initially flagged this as a significant payment-flow change; I worked with them to scope a phased approach — part-payment as a configuration flag on the checkout, not a new flow — which cut the build time from 4 weeks to 10 days.

Provider: Vertical Insure — third-party integration covering trip cancellations, medical emergencies, weather delays, and other unforeseen events. I led the vendor selection (evaluated three providers), wrote the integration spec, and coordinated the API contract review with engineering.

Cancellation transparency

Each trip in the cart shows the guide's cancellation window when the user expands the "Customize Trip" section — so customers can see exactly how long they have to cancel penalty-free before deciding whether to insure. This made the insurance decision more informed and reduced the friction of buying protection users didn't feel they needed.

Case Study 03

Programmatic Destination Pages: From Thin Pages to 60% of Organic Traffic

Guidesly · Series A Adventure Booking Platform · 2025

Shipped · Live at guidesly.com
60%
Of organic traffic through destination pages
142
Destination pages live
6 wks
Spec to live
Top 10
Destination pages rank among most visited on site

The Problem

Guidesly had basic location pages — just a list of guide cards with no location context, no breadcrumbs, no SEO structure, no schema validation, no meta tags, and no editorial content. They ranked poorly, converted poorly, and added no value beyond what the search page already offered.

Users searching "fishing charters in Islamorada" or "Galveston fishing guides" were landing on bare pages that gave them no reason to stay or book. The organic opportunity was being left entirely on the table — a direct revenue gap given that location-intent queries are the highest-converting segment in adventure travel.

I identified this through a combination of Heap traffic analysis, Google Search Console impression data, and a competitor audit. Destination pages on comparable platforms (FishingBooker, Viator) were ranking for thousands of location-intent keywords we had zero presence on. The fix was a template problem, not a content problem — which meant a single well-designed solution could scale to all 142 destinations at once.

Before

Basic guide card list only. No breadcrumbs, no schema markup, no meta tags, no location hero, no species info, no editorial content, no trust signals. Effectively invisible to search engines.

After

Rich destination pages with location hero, AI-generated review summaries, species section, FAQ, sort/filter, breadcrumbs, trust signals, full schema validation and meta tags. 142 pages live.

SEO Foundation

Proper schema markup, canonical tags, meta titles and descriptions, OG tags — built into the template so every page is SEO-ready from day one without manual intervention.

Scale by design

Template-driven architecture — one design, 142 pages. Adding a new destination requires no design or engineering work. Supply team adds guides; the page takes care of itself.

Tradeoff made

Chose programmatic templating over hand-crafted pages. Traded editorial uniqueness for scale and speed — the right call at Series A where supply coverage matters more than per-page polish.

How it came together

The engineering team's initial instinct was to build each destination page as a separate route with manually curated content. I pushed back — that would have required content ops resources we didn't have and wouldn't scale past ~20 pages. I specced a template-driven architecture where a single design drives all 142 pages, with guide listings, species data, and AI-generated review summaries pulled dynamically at render time. Supply team adds guides; the page auto-publishes.

I wrote full Figma wireframes for every section — location hero with booking widget, trust signal bar, guide listings, species cards with habitat and size data, editorial "why fish here" content, ratings summary, FAQ, and breadcrumb navigation. Critically, I embedded SEO requirements directly into the design brief: schema type per section, meta tag structure, heading hierarchy, canonical tag logic. This meant engineering had a single spec that covered both UX and technical SEO, eliminating a handoff gap that typically causes schema errors or missing tags post-launch.

The full build shipped in 6 weeks from spec to live. 142 pages indexed in the first crawl cycle.

Full interactive prototype: View Figma wireframes

Live destination page example: Islamorada Fishing Charters

Live product

Live at guidesly.com/destination

Islamorada, FL — one of 142 live destination pages. Location hero, guide listings with AI review summaries, species section, trust signals, sort and filter. Now among the top pages on the site by traffic.

Instrumentation & results

Before launch I built a Heap conversion funnel from destination pages through to booking — tracking CTA clicks, guide detail page visits, checkout starts, and completed bookings at the component level. This gave us a full drop-off view from first page visit to completed payment, not just aggregate traffic numbers, and let us identify that the guide card CTA was the primary conversion bottleneck post-SEO.

Within 90 days of launch, destination pages became the highest-volume organic acquisition channel on the site — ranking among the top 10 most visited pages. The template architecture paid forward: when supply team onboards a new destination, the page auto-publishes with full SEO structure — no design or engineering work required.

Case Study 04

WildCast: India's Outdoor Experience Marketplace

Independent Research Project · 2026

Research project · Prototypes built
WILDCAST
"Book the Wild" — wildcast.in
MarketIndia outdoor experiences
ModelTwo-sided marketplace
VerticalsTrekking · Camping · Wildlife · Watersports · Snow
Target GMV Y3₹75 Crore

The opportunity

India has 1.4 billion people, extraordinary ecological diversity, and zero dominant platform for booking outdoor recreation experiences. Online penetration of activity booking is below 3% — 97% of bookings still happen over phone calls and WhatsApp forwards.

WildCast is an independent research and product exploration — market sizing, competitive analysis, India-specific product strategy, and two fully interactive prototypes, developed to validate whether a multi-vertical outdoor marketplace could work in the Indian context.

The ₹75 Crore Y3 GMV target is built bottom-up: India domestic adventure tourism is a ₹15L Cr market growing at 17% CAGR. Taking a conservative 0.05% online capture in Year 3 — against a comparable platform benchmark of 0.1–0.2% at similar stage — yields ₹750 Crore TAM within reachable addressable market. At 10% platform take-rate, ₹75 Crore GMV translates to ~₹7.5 Crore net revenue, viable for a Series A raise at 8–10× revenue multiple in this segment.

India-specific unlock

WhatsApp-native booking. Full booking flow inside WhatsApp — no app download required. No global outdoor platform has done this.

India-specific unlock

Informal guide formalisation. 500,000+ informal guides — mahouts, river guides, jungle trackers — who have never appeared on any platform.

India-specific unlock

Hybrid payment model. 20–30% online to confirm, balance in cash on arrival. Solves operator GST anxiety and consumer trust in one move.

Strategic differentiation

Competitive analysis covered seven platforms: global (Viator, GetYourGuide, Airbnb Experiences), regional (Thrillophilia, Bikat Adventures, Holidify), and category-specific (India Hikes). None operate multi-vertical on a shared booking infrastructure. None have WhatsApp-native flows. None have addressed the 500K+ informal guide segment. Each is either too narrow (single-vertical), too city-centric (day tours), or too top-down (curated packages with no guide marketplace).

WildCast's structural advantage: multi-vertical from day one — trekking, camping, wildlife safaris, watersports, and snow sports on a shared infrastructure. Corporate offsites as a dedicated high-ticket vertical with 3–5× the average booking value of consumer trips. A conservation data layer (catch logs, sighting logs, wildlife footfall data) that compounds with every booking — creating a data moat no pure-play booking marketplace can replicate, and a potential licensing revenue stream from conservation organisations and researchers.

Case Study 05

Conversion Architecture: Closing the Gap Between Content and Bookings

Guidesly · Blog & Species Pages CRO · Phase 1 · 2026

Approved · In development · Expected Q2 2026
55%
Of organic traffic with zero booking CTAs
0
Booking CTAs on top 10 pages
>3%
Target CTA click-through post-fix
172
Keywords on top blog post — all driving traffic with no booking path

The Problem

A Semrush audit I ran in early 2026 revealed 8 of our top 10 pages by traffic were species and blog pages — with zero booking CTAs. The top blog post (trout fishing guide) pulled 3.21% of all site traffic across 172 keywords. The page ended. Users hit back. They booked elsewhere.

This was not a traffic problem — it was a conversion architecture problem hiding as a growth problem. Of our keyword mix, 61.8% were informational, but 10% were transactional (the highest-value segment). Every transactional-intent visitor arrived ready to book and found no path to do so.

The root cause was a template-level gap, not a content gap. Blog and species page templates had no CTA wiring at all. This meant one template fix would simultaneously fix every page on the site — a high-leverage change that justified prioritisation over feature work.

I presented this to leadership as a revenue recovery initiative, not a UX cleanup: "We have a leaking bucket. Every day this isn't fixed is bookings going to competitors." That framing moved it from the backlog to approved in one planning cycle.

SEO Audit Finding

61.8% of keywords are informational. 10% are transactional — the highest-value segment. None of those visits had a booking path.

Root Cause

Template-level gap — blog and species page templates had no CTA wiring. One template change touches every page on the site.

Key Design Decision

Pre-filtered CTAs, not generic /search links. CTA links to /search?species=trout — matching exactly what the user was reading. Generic links don't convert.

High-Intent Moment

The habitat map on species pages = "where can I fish for this?" moment. Destination chips below the map, pulled from live guide inventory for that species.

Component Spec — Dynamic Guide Card Strip

placement: After 3rd content section — peak engagement point in reading session.

accepts params: species=trout | location=montana | activity_type=fly_fishing

renders: 3 guide cards — name, location, price, next available date, Check Availability CTA.

fallback: If <3 guides for species in region, broaden to state-level. Never render empty strip.

reused on: Blog template + Species template. One component, two page types. Zero duplication.

Live product — programmatic destination pages

Live at guidesly.com/destination

Islamorada destination page — one of hundreds of programmatically generated location pages that auto-publish when a destination reaches 10+ verified guides. Pages include location-specific hero, guide listings with AI-generated review summaries, sort and filter controls, and trust signals. Destination pages now account for ~60% of organic traffic — the highest-volume acquisition channel on the site.

SEO audit (Semrush)CROTemplate architectureParameterised componentsContent freshness strategyHeap instrumentation

How I'll measure success

Pre-defined success criteria, agreed before development starts: primary metric is CTA click-through rate on the guide card strip, target >3% (industry benchmark for contextual in-content CTAs is 2–4%). Secondary metrics: bounce rate reduction on blog and species pages, and assisted booking attribution — sessions that touched a blog or species page within 7 days of a completed booking.

I instrumented the Heap tracking schema before the build kicked off, so we have a clean pre/post baseline and won't be reverse-engineering attribution post-launch. The same approach that worked in Case 3 (Search) — define the leading indicator first, let it prove out before reading conversion data.
